newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Argentaria net drops, but core roars back.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Argentaria net drops, but core roars back.

text.p: Spain's minority state-owned bank Argentaria reported a sharp drop in first-quarter earnings on Wednesday, but the stock soared as its core banking business rebounded in response to aggressive restructuring.

Argentaria, still 29.2 percent state-owned and due for further privatisation this year, reported net attributable profit fell 29.4 percent to 15.81 billion pesetas ($109.3 million) in the first-quarter, far worse than a Reuters consensus forecast for a 15.5 percent fall.

But the ragged bottom line disguised a sharp improvement in basic banking, as Argentaria's aggressive strategy to cut a mountain of low-yielding assets and expensive liabilities paid off with a well-received rise in net interest income.

Net income rose 13 percent to 53.80 billion pesetas, against average expectations for a 5.2 percent rise. Operating income rose 9.3 percent to 27.26 billion pesetas, against expectations for a slight decline, as the upper half of accounts, representing core banking, improved.
"We are satisfied," Argentaria spokesman Manuel Bueno told Reuters. "The top part shows that we are doing fine."
Pre-tax earnings would have risen 6.7 percent in the first quarter excluding extraordinary expenses, said Javier Bernat, analyst at brokerage Inverban, highlighting the turnaround.
"The bottom line is worse than expected," Bernat said. "But typical banking business is developing positively. The bank is recuperating margin both relatively and absolutely."

Argentaria, formed in 1991 in a merger of six state-owned banks and savings banks, embarked last year on an aggressive campaign to boost sagging profitability by restructuring assets and liabilities and expanding a small domestic network.
In December, Argentaria devoted nearly half its 1996 pre-tax profits to deal with these pressing problems and analysts said these results were signs of a rebound.
"These are good results," said Jose Sevilla, banking analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid. "It seems that the fall in operating results has come to an end."
Sevilla predicted smooth operating results for the remainder of the year, as the group continues to tackle problems.
Argentaria will press ahead with the restructuring of its Banco Exterior unit, which has been hampered by large staff numbers at above-average salaries and is seen as a key weakness.

Though not set yet, the plan could cut staffing levels by 1,500 persons in the next three years through early retirement and similar schemes, Argentaria's Bueno said. Banco Exterior has a fund of 106 billion pesetas to cover related costs, he added.
In the first quarter Argentaria set up Gesinor to sell 175 billion pesetas in properties acquired through non-payment of loans.
It will also pursue prudent expansion abroad with its 280 billion peseta fund. It is looking at Mexico, Colombia and other countries although no announcements are expected short-term, Bueno said.
But not everyone was convinced that Argentaria's results meant the group had put its problems behind it.
"I'm surprised people are so excited," a London-based analyst said. "Analysts were going for low net interest income."
Given the reduction of costly liabilities tied to the Official Credit Institute last year and a prepayment of other liabilities in December, net interest income should been better, he said.
